meta.title: Scienteens Lab · From Mersenne to Kundt
meta.description: A sound workshop for students around age 15: follow a wave in a spring, explore standing waves and measure the speed of sound with a Kundt tube.

hero.title: The Kundt tube workshop
hero.introduction: A distant cannon flashes before we hear it. How can that delay tell us the speed of sound? We begin with Mersenne’s experiments, use a spring to see how a wave travels, then measure a wavelength in a Kundt tube.

interview.title: From Mersenne to Kundt
interview.summary: Students follow a disturbance, identify standing waves and use the spacing between their nodes to measure the speed of sound.

steps.title: Measuring the speed of sound
paragraphs: When a distant cannon fires, we see the flash before hearing the report. Sound takes time to reach us, and the delay grows with the distance. Light travels so much faster that, for this experiment, the flash effectively marks the instant of firing.

Marin Mersenne investigated the speed of sound in the seventeenth century, alongside his work on vibrating strings and music. In Harmonie universelle, published in 1636, he described experiments with cannon fire and echoes. These methods connected a sound’s travel time with a distance that could be measured.

If the cannon is at a distance D and the sound arrives after a delay Δt, its speed is v = D / Δt. An echo needs a different distance: the sound travels to the reflecting wall and back. For a wall at distance D, the total path is 2D, so v = 2D / Δt.

A short delay is difficult to time by hand. A longer path gives a larger delay, which is easier to distinguish. The distance still has to be known: an accurate timing measurement cannot compensate for an incorrect distance.

A Kundt tube brings the experiment into the classroom. We use a known frequency and measure a wavelength, so there is no short travel time to record. Before using this method, we need to understand what a sound wave is.

media.alt: Historical engraving of Mersenne and Pierre Petit looking upward beside a cannon aimed vertically.
media.title: Mersenne and Petit’s cannon experiment
media.caption: Mersenne and Petit study the motion of a cannonball. Cannon fire also provides two signals for measuring sound speed: a flash at firing and a report heard after a delay.

references.label: François Baskevitch, Calculer la vitesse du son après Newton : le défi du jeune Euler, pp. 5 to 6

steps.title: We know its speed. What is sound?
paragraphs: When a bell rings, the bell vibrates but stays where it is. We can hear it across the room. What happens in the air between the bell and our ears?

This question was already discussed in antiquity. In De Anima, Aristotle connected sound with an impact and the motion of air between an object and the ear. His account raises a question we can investigate experimentally: how does motion at a source produce a change at a distance?

A vibrating object disturbs the surrounding air. Pressure variations spread away from it and set the eardrum in motion when they reach the ear. A microphone also responds to pressure variations, converting them into an electrical signal that we can record.

The video compares sound travelling the same distance through air, water and steel. Before watching, predict the order of arrival. Since the distance is the same, the earliest arrival corresponds to the greatest propagation speed.

Sound is a mechanical wave: its transmission depends on interactions within a material. It can travel through gases, liquids and solids, but not through a vacuum. Light can travel through a vacuum. To examine mechanical propagation directly, we will use a spring whose motion is easy to see.

media.title: The speed of sound depends on the medium
media.caption: The distance is the same in all three media. Compare the arrival times to rank their sound speeds.

source.label: Aristotle, De Anima, Book II, Chapter 8

steps.title: From a pulse to a standing wave
paragraphs: A wave is a disturbance that propagates. In a spring, the disturbance is a change in the position of the coils. In air, sound involves changes in pressure and density. For a mechanical wave, neighbouring parts of the material exert forces on one another, allowing the disturbance to spread.
A Slinky makes two motions visible: the movement of one coil and the movement of a compression along the spring. Following them separately helps us distinguish local motion from propagation.
A brief push produces a pulse. Regular oscillation produces a periodic wave. When the wave reaches an end, it is reflected; the incident and reflected waves can overlap to form a standing wave.

substeps.title: A travelling pulse
substeps.text: Give one end of a stretched Slinky a short push along its length. Before trying it, predict whether a coil will travel with the compression. Follow the compressed region, then repeat while watching one marked coil.

media.alt: Animation of a hand creating a longitudinal pulse in a horizontal spring.
media.title: Following a compression and a coil
media.caption: Watch one coil as the compression passes. Its motion is local; the compressed region travels along the spring.

paragraphs: The compression travels along the spring. The marked coil moves as the pulse passes, then returns near its initial position. Neighbouring coils move closer together and separate again: the changing spacing is the disturbance that propagates.

The coils move parallel to the direction of propagation. This is a longitudinal wave. Sound in air is also longitudinal: its acoustic motion is along the direction in which compressions and rarefactions travel.

The moving coils have kinetic energy, and deformation of the spring stores elastic potential energy. A moving section deforms its neighbour and exerts a force on it. Energy is passed along the spring through these interactions, while each section moves only locally.

substeps.title: Sound propagation, wavelength and frequency
substeps.text: What makes the next coil move? Compressing one section changes the elastic forces on its neighbours. Their motion changes the forces farther along, so the disturbance spreads from section to section.
paragraphs: The spring’s elasticity tends to restore the spacing of the coils. The coils also have mass: a force changes their velocity rather than moving them instantaneously into a new position. Elasticity and inertia together determine how fast the disturbance propagates.

A loudspeaker sets up a similar transmission in air. As its membrane moves forward, it compresses the nearby air and raises its pressure. The pressure difference accelerates neighbouring air, which changes the pressure farther away. As the membrane moves back, the nearby air expands and its pressure falls. This region of lower pressure is a rarefaction. Repeated motion produces successive compressions and rarefactions.

Small portions of air move back and forth locally as the wave passes. The compression can cross the room while this acoustic motion remains close to equilibrium. The animation’s dots represent that collective motion. Individual gas molecules also have rapid random motion, which is not shown here.

In the eighteenth century, Euler studied vibrating strings mathematically by considering the motion of interacting parts. Our spring makes this transmission visible: a disturbance spreads through the forces between neighbouring sections.

For a periodic wave, frequency f counts complete oscillations per second and is measured in hertz. The period T is the time for one oscillation, so T = 1 / f. The wavelength λ is the distance between successive compressions, or between successive rarefactions.
During one period, the wave travels one wavelength. Its speed is therefore v = λ / T. Substituting T = 1 / f gives v = fλ: propagation speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.

For sound in air under fixed conditions, the speed is approximately the same across these frequencies. Doubling the frequency therefore halves the wavelength. In the Kundt experiment, we set the frequency and measure the wavelength to determine the speed.

source.label: Leonhard Euler, De vibratione chordarum exercitatio

media.alt: A loudspeaker produces compressions in dots representing small portions of air.
media.title: A periodic disturbance in air
media.caption: The dots oscillate locally. Follow a compression as it travels away from the source; the distance to the next compression is one wavelength.

media.alt: Animation comparing several periodic patterns with different spatial repetitions.
media.title: Different wavelengths in the same medium
media.caption: Count the repetitions within the same distance. A shorter wavelength corresponds to a higher frequency when propagation speed is unchanged.

substeps.title: Transverse waves and their graphs
substeps.text: Move one end of the Slinky sideways, perpendicular to its length. The coils now move across the direction of propagation: this is a transverse wave. A vibrating guitar string provides another example.

media.alt: Diagram comparing compressions in a longitudinal wave with the sinusoidal representation of a transverse wave.
media.title: Longitudinal and transverse waves
media.caption: Compare the direction of local motion with the direction of propagation: parallel for a longitudinal wave, perpendicular for a transverse wave.

media.alt: Diagram showing wavelength measured horizontally between two equivalent points of a transverse wave.
media.title: Measuring wavelength on a transverse wave
media.caption: One wavelength separates neighbouring crests. Measure it along the direction of propagation, rather than along the curved shape of the wave.

paragraphs: On a snapshot of the spring, a crest and a trough are the greatest displacements on opposite sides of equilibrium. Amplitude is the greatest displacement from equilibrium. Wavelength is measured along the spring, from one crest to the next or from one trough to the next.

A graph against position shows the spring at one instant and lets us measure wavelength. A graph against time follows one coil and lets us measure its period. The curves can look similar, so the horizontal axis tells us which measurement is possible.

A sinusoidal curve can also represent sound pressure. Its height then gives a pressure variation, rather than a vertical movement of the air. A pressure maximum marks a compression and a minimum a rarefaction. The air’s acoustic motion is still along the direction of propagation.

For a pure tone, increasing frequency raises pitch. Increasing sound-pressure amplitude generally makes it louder. On a periodic microphone recording, the time between repetitions gives the period; the size of the signal reflects the pressure variation.

substeps.title: Reflection at a fixed end
substeps.text: The string’s right end is held by a clamp. Before watching, predict what an upward pulse will look like after it reaches this end and travels back.

media.title: A pulse reflected at a fixed end
media.caption: Compare the incident and reflected pulses. Follow a blue point to distinguish its local motion from the pulse’s travel.

credit.label: Recording of Wave on a String, PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder.

paragraphs: The upward pulse travels towards the clamp. After reflection, it returns as a downward pulse. The pulse has reversed both its direction of travel and the sign of its displacement. The blue points continue moving locally as the pulse passes.

The clamp holds the end at zero displacement. At this point, the incident and reflected displacements must cancel. An upward incident displacement therefore requires an equal downward reflected displacement: this fixed boundary explains the inversion.

The pulse also reflects at the left end once the source has returned to rest. In this recording, damping is set to zero, so it continues travelling back and forth. On a real string, some energy is dissipated and the pulse gradually weakens.

Sound reflects too. At a rigid wall, air cannot move through the boundary, so the air displacement is constrained. Pressure behaves differently: a compression reflects as a compression. We must therefore say whether a diagram represents displacement or pressure when describing a reflection.

substeps.title: Superposition and standing modes
substeps.text: What happens when the source keeps oscillating while its reflected wave returns? Drive the Slinky regularly and vary the frequency. Look for positions that stay at equilibrium throughout a complete cycle.
paragraphs: Where two disturbances overlap, their displacements add. Displacements in the same direction reinforce each other; opposite displacements reduce or cancel each other. For small disturbances, each wave continues propagating after the overlap. This is superposition.

A continuously driven wave overlaps with its reflection. Two waves of equal amplitude, with the same frequency and wavelength, travelling in opposite directions form an ideal standing wave. Its pattern stays in place while the sections between its nodes oscillate.
A displacement node stays at zero displacement throughout the cycle. At an antinode, the oscillation amplitude is greatest. Sections on opposite sides of a node move in opposite directions.
Neighbouring nodes are separated by λ / 2. A node and its nearest antinode are separated by λ / 4. A point that briefly crosses equilibrium is not necessarily a node: follow it for a full cycle.

At certain driving frequencies, the response becomes much stronger. This is resonance: the source is driving close to one of the system’s natural frequencies. The standing modes must satisfy the constraints at both ends, so the length and end conditions determine which wavelengths fit.

A real spring loses energy through damping. Continued driving maintains the oscillation, and the response at resonance remains finite. A well-established pattern makes the nodes easier to locate and their spacing easier to measure.

substeps.title: Standing waves on a guitar string
substeps.text: In Giancoli’s illustration, compare the open string with the string pressed against a fret. Predict how shortening the vibrating section will change the note.
paragraphs: A guitar string is approximately fixed at both ends of its vibrating length L. Each end is a displacement node. In the fundamental mode, half a wavelength fits between them: λ₁ = 2L. This gives f₁ = vₛ / (2L), where vₛ is wave speed along the string.

Pressing a fret shortens the vibrating section. If tension and mass per unit length remain nearly unchanged, wave speed stays nearly the same, so the shorter wavelength produces a higher frequency. At the twelfth fret, the length is halved and the fundamental frequency doubles: the note rises by an octave.

The string transfers motion through the bridge to the soundboard, which sets the surrounding air in motion. The string’s wave is transverse; the sound wave in air is longitudinal. They share the vibration’s frequency, but their speeds and wavelengths are different.
The fixed ends determine the string’s allowed standing modes. We will use the same displacement constraint to find the modes of a tube with rigid, closed ends.

media.alt: Giancoli’s guitar illustration: (a) an open string in its fundamental standing mode; (b) a finger presses a fret and shortens the vibrating section between the fret and bridge.
media.title: An open string and a fingered string
media.caption: The two curves show opposite extremes of the fundamental mode. The fret shortens the section that can vibrate.

source.label: Giancoli, Physics: Principles with Applications, 7th edition, section 12-4, pp. 336 to 337

steps.title: From Chladni figures to a closed tube
paragraphs: How can a vibration reveal its own pattern? Chladni sprinkled sand on a plate and set it vibrating with a bow. He published his investigations in 1787. The grains moved across the plate and gathered into patterns that changed with the mode.

Sand tends to leave the strongly vibrating regions and collect along nodal lines, where the plate moves very little. The plate’s vibration is two-dimensional. In a narrow tube, we can study the air’s standing-wave pattern mainly along its length.

Take an ideal tube of length L with two rigid, closed ends. Air cannot move through either wall, so each end is a displacement node. In the fundamental mode, half a wavelength fits between these nodes: L = λ₁ / 2. Higher modes fit n half-wavelengths into the same length, giving L = nλₙ / 2 and λₙ = 2L / n.

Substituting into v = fλ gives fₙ = nv / (2L), with n = 1, 2, 3, … . The resonant frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental f₁ = v / (2L). Predict what happens to f₁ when the tube’s length doubles, then check using this expression.

At a closed end, the air cannot move, but its pressure can vary. This position is a displacement node and a pressure antinode. At a displacement antinode, the pressure variation is smallest: it is a pressure node. The two patterns have their nodes at different positions.

A microphone measures pressure variation. Its largest signal therefore identifies a pressure antinode, which corresponds to a displacement node. Our loudspeaker moves to drive the air, so the rigid-end tube is an approximate model of the apparatus. Its predicted frequencies guide the experiment; the wavelength comes from the measured spacing.

media.alt: Historical line drawing of a vibrating plate sprinkled with sand and excited with a bow.
media.title: Making nodal lines visible
media.caption: The sand marks nodal lines, where the plate’s motion is small. Changing the mode changes the pattern.

source.label: E. F. F. Chladni, Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges (1787)

references.label: OpenStax, Normal Modes of a Standing Sound Wave

steps.title: Kundt’s tube: measuring a wavelength
paragraphs: In 1866, August Kundt described acoustic dust figures and their use in measuring sound speed in gases and solids. A vibrating rod drove the gas in his tube, and light powder formed a repeated pattern. Measuring the spacing of this pattern gave the gas wavelength.
A loudspeaker drives the air in the tube at a frequency we can control. We first find a strong resonant response, then move a microphone along the tube to locate the pressure nodes and antinodes.

The microphone measures pressure oscillations. A pressure node gives a small signal; a pressure antinode gives a large one. Two neighbouring nodes are separated by half a wavelength, and the same is true of two neighbouring antinodes. We must compare positions of the same kind: a node and its nearest antinode are only a quarter-wavelength apart.

Light grains provide another way to reveal the tube’s spatial pattern. We measure the spacing between repeated deposits and compare it with the microphone measurements. The deposits show a repeated pattern; they do not trace the motion of individual air particles.
For dry air at 22.8 °C, an ideal-gas calculation gives a speed of about 345 m/s. Our result is close to this value.

The same method can be used with another gas. At a fixed frequency, a different wavelength means a different speed of sound. Mersenne measured a distance and a travel time; here, we measure a wavelength and use the frequency set at the source.

source.label: August Kundt, On a New Kind of Acoustic Dust Figures (1866)

game.title: The Resonance Lab
game.description: Identify the tube’s end conditions, then find its resonances by varying frequency. Compare the modes you discover. In the Kundt activity, measure the spacing between deposits and use v = 2fd to calculate sound speed.
